content: The International Association for the Surgery of Trauma and Surgical Intensive Care (IATSIC) was established in 1988. Its primary objective is to create a platform for the exchange of information and the development of new knowledge in the fields of trauma surgery and surgical intensive care. This is achieved through clinical experience and laboratory research. The association fulfills its mission by organizing scientific meetings, publishing relevant materials, and conducting training courses. IATSIC operates as an integrated society within the larger International Society of Surgery (Société Internationale de Chirurgie), which was founded in 1902 and currently has over 3,000 members across 80 countries. IATSIC itself comprises 270 members from 53 countries, representing every continent. Its membership includes surgeons in good professional standing who have a significant interest and active practice in trauma surgery and/or surgical intensive care. Contributions to scientific literature in these fields are also a key criterion for membership. The World Health Organization (WHO) was founded in 1948 as a specialized agency of the United Nations, serving as the directing and coordinating authority for international health matters and public health. One of WHO’s constitutional functions is to provide objective and reliable information and advice in the field of human health. This responsibility is partially fulfilled through its extensive publication program. WHO’s publications aim to support national health strategies and address the most pressing public health concerns globally. To meet the needs of member states at all levels of development, WHO produces practical manuals, handbooks, and training materials for specific categories of health workers, as well as internationally applicable guidelines and standards. It also publishes reviews and analyses of health policies, programs, and research, along with state-of-the-art consensus reports offering technical advice and recommendations for decision-makers. These publications are closely aligned with WHO’s priority activities, which include disease prevention and control, the development of equitable health systems based on primary health care, and health promotion for individuals and communities. Injury is an increasingly significant global health problem. Every day, 16,000 people die from injuries, and for every person who dies, several thousand more are injured, many with permanent sequelae. Injuries account for 16% of the global burden of disease, with the majority of this burden—approximately 90%—occurring in lowand middle-income countries. Reducing the burden of injuries is one of the main public health challenges of this century. WHO plays a critical role in addressing this challenge, particularly through its Department of Injuries and Violence Prevention (VIP). This department has led efforts to improve injury control activities, including standardizing injury surveillance systems, promoting injury control policies for violence and traffic-related injuries, and advocating for low-cost improvements in injury care in both pre-hospital and hospital settings. The Essential Trauma Care (EsTC) Project focuses on promoting cost-effective improvements in facility-based trauma care. Alongside WHO’s guidelines for pre-hospital trauma care, the EsTC Project aims to ensure a minimum standard of care for injured individuals worldwide. The potential benefits of these improvements are highlighted by the stark disparities in outcomes between lowand middle-income countries and high-income countries. For example, individuals with life-threatening but treatable injuries are six times more likely to die in low-income settings (36% mortality) compared to high-income settings (6% mortality). The Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care aim to reduce these disparities by establishing achievable and affordable standards for injury care globally. These guidelines outline essential trauma services and the human and physical resources required to provide them. The guidelines were developed collaboratively with the International Association for the Surgery of Trauma and Surgical Intensive Care (IATSIC) and other international and national societies, as well as numerous experts actively involved in trauma care worldwide. The guidelines emphasize that improved outcomes for injured patients can be achieved through better organization and planning of trauma care services. These improvements are considered cost-effective, feasible, and sustainable, even in resource-limited settings. IATSIC members are available to assist in implementing these guidelines in partnership with WHO, governments, health authorities, and medical institutions. The ultimate goal is to improve the care of injured individuals worldwide.
